source.title_on_document: Experimental Evidence on the Productivity Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence

supplement.where: Supplementary Materials referred to throughout the main text (p. 3, p. 4, p. 5); no URL given in the document. Data and code on OSF: https://osf.io/xd7qw/
supplement.holds: Separate statistics for the overall grade and the writing-quality, content-quality, and originality sub-grades (the main text gives only 'similar increases'); full design description and questionnaires; objective time measures; Lee bounds and controls for employment status and occupation; 2SLS estimates adjusting for imperfect compliance; the fixed-time (15-minute) arm details; grades of raw ChatGPT output compared with treated participants' grades; ChatGPT-usage detection and editing analysis.

paper_design_summary: 453 college-educated professionals recruited on Prolific each completed two occupation-specific, incentivized writing tasks (press releases, short reports, analysis plans, delicate emails). Between the tasks, half were randomly assigned to register for ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) and told they could use it on the second task; the control group registered for Overleaf. Blinded professionals from the same occupations graded each output on a 1-7 scale (overall grade plus writing quality, content quality, and originality sub-grades); time taken was also measured.

studies.label: Online experiment with professionals on occupation-specific writing tasks

assignment.what_was_assigned: Access to ChatGPT (instructed to register between task 1 and task 2 and permitted to use it on task 2) versus registering for Overleaf (not told they could use it). Incentive scheme (linear, convex, fixed 15-minute time) was cross-randomized.
assignment.quote: We randomly assigned 50% of participants to the treatment group and the remainder to the control group. The treatment group was instructed to register for ChatGPT between the first and second task
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 1 abstract ('In a preregistered online experiment'); p. 11, Data and materials availability: AEA RCT Registry https://www.socialscienceregistry.org/trials/10882

arms.name: Treatment (ChatGPT)
arms.description: Task 1 without AI; registered for ChatGPT, received guidance on using it, and was told it could use it on task 2. 92% registered and 80% used it on task 2 (p. 4).

arms.name: Control (Overleaf)
arms.description: Task 1 and task 2 without AI; registered for the LaTeX editor Overleaf between tasks to equalize sign-up costs; not told it could use Overleaf. About 10-20% of the control group used ChatGPT on the tasks (p. 4).

participants.exclusions: Attrition was 6% in the control group and 11% in the treatment group (p. 3, lines 35-36). The number analyzed for the grade outcome is not stated in this PDF. Figure 1 restricts to the linear and convex incentive groups, about 80% of respondents (p. 4 lines 27-28; p. 12 note). Arm counts 235 (control) and 218 (treatment) are the Table 1 N for the occupation rows, which sum to 453; Table 1 average task-1 grade has N 233 and 211.
participants.who: Experienced, college-educated professionals: marketers, grant writers, consultants, data analysts, human resource professionals, and managers
participants.quote: we recruited 453 experienced, college-educated professionals on the survey platform Prolific and assigned each to complete two occupation-specific, incentivized writing tasks

ai_tool.how_used: Treated participants could use ChatGPT freely on the second task. Most submitted lightly edited or unedited ChatGPT output: 33% reported submitting the initial output unedited and 53% reported editing (p. 5).

task.description: Occupation-specific professional writing tasks resembling real work: press releases, short reports, analysis plans, and delicate emails. Graded for overall quality, writing quality, content quality, and originality. The task is professional writing rather than a creative task; it enters scope only through the originality sub-grade.
task.duration: 20- to 30-minute assignments; a fixed-time incentive arm (20% of participants) required exactly 15 minutes per task

outcomes.name: Originality sub-grade from blinded occupation-matched evaluators
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Blinded experienced professionals from the same occupations gave specific grades for originality alongside the overall grade; each output seen by three evaluators. Scale for the sub-grade not stated in this PDF.

contrasts.reported: No numbers in this PDF. Text: 'Average evaluator grades in the treatment group increased by 0.45 standard deviations (p<0.001), with similar increases for overall grades and specific grades for writing quality, content quality, and originality.' Statistics are in the Supplementary Materials, not on file.

outcomes.name: Average evaluator grade (1-7) on the second task
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Blinded experienced professionals in the same occupations graded outputs 1-7 as if encountered at work, incentivized on agreement with other evaluators; three evaluators per output, average within-essay cross-evaluator correlation 0.44. Effect estimated from a participant-evaluator-level regression of the within-participant pre-to-post change on treatment, occupation*task-order FE, incentive-arm FE, and grader FE, SEs clustered by person, rescaled to pre-treatment SDs. Robustness in supplement: Lee bounds, controls for employment and occupation, 2SLS. The text distinguishes 'average evaluator grades' from 'overall grades'; the overall grade's own statistic is in the supplement.

contrasts.reported: Text: average evaluator grades increased by 0.45 SD (p<0.001). Figure 1B (linear and convex incentive groups): Treatment Effect 0.41 SDs, 95% CI [0.23, 0.59]. Figure 1D second-task grade: Control mean 3.802, Treatment mean 4.53. Abstract: output quality rose by 18%.
contrasts.locator: p. 1 abstract; p. 4, lines 18-20; p. 12, Fig. 1 panels B and D and note

contrasts.reported: In the fixed-time arm (20% of participants), 'the treatment increased grades by a similar albeit not statistically significant 0.33 standard deviations'; note 26: the confidence interval includes zero and the arms differ in average pre-treatment grades.

eligibility.reason: People were randomly assigned to ChatGPT access (p. 3); 453 were recruited and assigned, with attrition of 6% and 11% (p. 3), so the analyzed count is well above 50 though not stated. Blinded occupation-matched professionals graded originality on the output (p. 4). Borderline on scope: the tasks are professional writing (press releases, reports, emails) and the study is about productivity; creativity enters only through the originality sub-grade, whose numbers sit in the supplement, not in this PDF.

one_line_finding: Random ChatGPT access raised blinded professional graders' average grades by 0.45 SD (p<0.001; Fig. 1B 0.41 SD, 95% CI [0.23, 0.59]) with 'similar increases' for the originality sub-grade, and cut time by 11 minutes (p. 4, p. 12).
open_questions: Whether occupation-specific professional writing graded partly on originality counts as a creative task under the codebook's scope.
The originality sub-grade statistics and the number of people analyzed are in the Supplementary Materials, which are not on file.
The text's 0.45 SD and Figure 1B's 0.41 SD differ; Figure 1B restricts to the linear and convex incentive groups. Which sample gives 0.45 is not stated in this PDF.
Whether 235 and 218 (Table 1 occupation-row Ns) are the arm counts at assignment; they sum to the 453 recruited.
notes: Outcomes not listed because they bear on none of the three questions: time taken (self-reported and objective), grade inequality (Fig. 2A control slope 0.414, change in slope -0.272, 95% CI [-0.14, -0.405]), job satisfaction, self-efficacy, beliefs about automation (Fig. 3), and follow-up ChatGPT use at two weeks and two months (self-reported). The supplement also compares treated participants' grades with grades of raw ChatGPT output (no higher, p. 5); no numbers in this PDF. A further intervention let 30% of the treatment group edit or replace their task-1 output with ChatGPT (p. 4); no output outcome reported. Noncompliance: about 10-20% of controls used ChatGPT and 80% of treated used it, so the authors call the estimates lower bounds on the effect of usage (p. 4).
